title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
hookLine: I set before you life and death: choose life
carry: near, in your mouth and in your heart
last: CARRIED, EVEN WHEN IT DIDN'T FEEL LIKE IT.

cards: Plenty of the choices that shape a life don't feel like choices at all. They feel like Tuesday. Text back, or let it slide.
Bed, or one more episode. The true thing, or the easy one. Each one is tiny, but laid end to end, they become a direction.
Moses is near the end of his great speech in Deuteronomy. Now he boils it all down to a single choice, and sets it in front of his people like two plates on a table.

teach.h: LIFE AND GOOD, DEATH AND EVIL.
teach.b: Here's how Moses says it, in the King James Bible: "See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil."

A few verses on, he calls witnesses: "I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live."
In Hebrew: u-vacharta ba-chayyim, and you shall choose life.

Chayyim, life, is plural in form, and some readers hear in that plural that life is always more than one thing: breath and family and land and God, all at once. It's the same word as in the Jewish toast, l'chaim, to life.
Notice what Moses doesn't do. He doesn't choose for them. He sets it out, and he pleads.
And just before this, he says how possible it is. It isn't too hard for you, or far away, up in heaven or across the sea.

teach.h: THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.
teach.b: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it."
Then Moses says what life is: loving God, listening to his voice, holding on to him, "for he is thy life, and the length of thy days."
Paul quotes the word is nigh thee in his letter to the Romans, and some Christian readers hear an echo of the two ways in Jesus' words about two roads, one narrow.
And notice how often Moses says this day. The choice isn't saved for the end. It's on the table today.

how: Some Christians turn to Deuteronomy 30 when speaking about daily decisions and moral choices, and Paul quotes 'the word is nigh thee' from this chapter in Romans 10.

o: Moses' plea: life and death set before you, pick life
a rule to keep the body healthy with food and rest
a vow the priests took before serving at the altar

games.q: what's inside Moses' plea — tap the pairs.
p: life, a plural word in Hebrew
very nigh, in thy mouth and heart

s: Moses says the good way is far off, across the sea
the opposite: "the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart."
the Hebrew word for life is plural
chayyim, the same word as the toast l'chaim, to life.
Moses makes the choice for the people
he sets life and death before them, and pleads: choose life.

games.q: Moses has set two plates before you: life and good, death and evil. what's the next thing he says?
o: the choice is too hard for you.
games.why: therefore choose life, "that both thou and thy seed may live". he doesn't decide for them. he pleads.

practice: Think ahead through the rest of your day and find one small fork, two plates on the table, where one choice leaves you or someone else a little more alive: a walk instead of the scroll, the kind answer instead of the clever one.
Picture yourself choosing life there. If you pray, ask for help to choose it.

wordCard.voice: Choose life. Moses' plea near the end of Deuteronomy: life and death are set before you, and the word is near, in your mouth and in your heart.
